item.title: 3 Films in Which the Body Holds What the Mind Can't
item.description:
Media

3 Films in Which the Body Holds What the Mind Can't

Interoceptive awareness explains why feelings surface as physical sensation.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Interoceptive awareness, sometimes called the "eighth sense," helps us read our body's internal signals.
  • People with PTSD may show lower prefrontal cortex activation and reduced body awareness.
  • Films like 'Black Swan' and 'The Wrestler' show characters' bodies revealing pain before their minds do.

When we don’t have the words to tell someone what happened to us, our bodies just step in. For instance, when we are grieving, we might say, “My heart is heavy” because that is how it feels in our body. When you are anxious, you might say, “My stomach is in knots” because the feeling of anxiety lies in our stomach.

Feelings can be so intense that we experience the sensation in our bodies before we can cognitively explain them. In psychology, we call this interoceptive awareness — sometimes referred to as our “eighth sense.” It is how we understand our body’s internal physical signals (heartbeat, breathing, or temperature) when something feels misaligned.

In the book The Body Keeps the Score, Bessel van der Kolk explained how trauma can reshape our bodies and brains. He found that individuals with PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) have trouble processing sensations in their bodies. He also shows a connection between little-to-no interoceptive awareness and low activation in the prefrontal cortex. In other words, the trauma we feel could change our brain’s fear response and wreak havoc on our nervous systems.

If we learn to pay attention to our body’s signals in a mindful, present way by focusing on nonjudgmental awareness and acceptance of bodily sensations, we can reconnect the mind and body. In a 2020 research study, a 16-week yoga program was compared to a 16-week wellness lifestyle program for treating PTSD symptoms. The yoga program, which focused on the body, physical postures (asanas), controlled breathing (pranayama), and meditation, was more beneficial in reducing symptoms of PTSD and stress. The participants in the yoga program developed greater interoceptive, somatic, and emotional awareness, as well as self-regulation, than those in the wellness program, which offered walking, stress-reduction workshops, and nutritional counseling.

Following are three award-winning movies in which the protagonist’s body reacts before the mind catches up, in a way that is eerily truthful and sometimes gut-wrenching.

Black Swan
Source: Fox Searchlight Pictures

Black Swan (2010): The body of Nina (Natalie Portman) physically deteriorates in front of us as the pressure in her life builds and her mental state collapses. While her brain doesn’t process what is happening to her, her body transforms into something else – something she has rejected, something horrific, frail, fierce, and destroyed.

Manchester by the Sea
Source: Amazon Studios

Manchester by the Sea (2016): Lee Chandler (Casey Affleck) is emotionally shut down, following the tragic death of his children in a house fire caused by his own negligence. Lee is so consumed by an unbearable amount of guilt that he is living in an embodied state of perpetual numbness.

The Wrestler
Source: Fox Searchlight

The Wrestler (2008): Mickey Rourke portrays Randy, whose body becomes a metaphor for his ruined life. His self-inflicted damage on his body as a wrestler is a physical manifestation of his self-loathing and lack of self-worth.
